papers.title: Do Commercial Property Taxes Affect Business Microlocation Decisions?
papers.authors: Brayden D. Bulloch, Fabio B. Gaertner, Jeffrey L. Hoopes
papers.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  Do commercial property taxes affect business microlocation decisions? Using precise geolocations for 2.8 million U.S. establishments, we employ a spatial discontinuity density design, comparing for-profit establishments to nonprofits, which are generally exempt from property taxes. Relative to nonprofit establishments, for-profit establishments disproportionately locate on the low-tax side of county borders. This effect strengthens with the size of the tax differential. At borders with differentials in the top decile (quartile), we estimate a 6–7 (5–6) percent shift in establishment location toward the low-tax side over a 10-km band. Businesses move from as far as 10 km away on the high-tax side but concentrate within 1 km on the low-tax side. Firms trade off tax savings with customer access: low-foot-traffic establishments respond more to tax differentials than high-foot-traffic ones. A survey of U.S. mayors finds that perceptions of property taxes’ importance for business location rise with cross-border tax differentials.
                  Data Availability: Survey data are available upon request. All other data were obtained from publicly and commercially available sources described in the manuscript.
                  JEL Classifications: H25; H71; H73; R32.

papers.title: Unwinding Loan Prospecting Pressure through Renegotiation: The Role of Loan Officer Changes in Debt Contracting
papers.authors: Jessie Cheong, Jung Koo Kang, Regina Wittenberg-Moerman
papers.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  We examine the impact of loan officer changes on debt contract design. Loan officers face pressure to originate new loans, incentivizing them to offer loan terms that are more favorable than warranted by borrowers’ creditworthiness. Because a loan officer who replaces the originating loan officer is not subject to this loan prospecting pressure, we predict that she reverses the favorable discretion exercised at loan origination. Consistent with this prediction, we find that the first renegotiation following the replacement of the originating loan officer is associated with more unfavorable renegotiation outcomes. This effect is more pronounced when loan prospecting pressure at loan origination is greater—when the originating loan officer is less experienced, when the lead arranger faces tight performance benchmarks or lower income growth, and when credit market competition is more intense. Overall, we provide novel insights into how loan officer changes restore contracting efficiency through renegotiations.
                  Data Availability: Syndicated loan data are from DealScan; borrower financial data are from Compustat and CRSP; bank financial data are from the Call Report and Compustat; loan agreements are from Morningstar, FactSet, and SEC filings; analyst data are from I/B/E/S; credit rating data are from S&P Global Ratings and the Mergent Fixed Income Securities Database (FISD); media coverage data are from RavenPack; covenant violation data are from Nini, Smith, and Sufi (2012); and loan officer employment histories were hand collected from LinkedIn.
                  JEL Classifications: G21; G30; G32; J24.

papers.title: Tax-Related Key Audit Matters and Changes in Multinational Income Shifting
papers.authors: Christof Beuselinck, Nathan C. Goldman, Jochen Pierk, Cinthia Valle Ruiz
papers.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  Key audit matters (KAMs) increase the salience of uncertainty surrounding the underlying accounts. We examine KAMs related to uncertain tax positions (UTPs), which highlight potential concerns to external stakeholders about uncertain tax planning activities such as multinational income shifting. Increased scrutiny may reduce the expected benefits of these strategies and discourage firms from pursuing them. Using KAM disclosures in the expanded audit reports, we find that group-level KAM disclosures are associated with a decline in multinational income shifting when the KAMs relate to UTPs. This relation is stronger when firms are financially unconstrained, when the institutional environment features strong tax enforcement, and when KAMs highlight specific risk statements and auditors provide explicit assurance. Overall, our findings reveal a novel and potentially unintended real effect of expanded audit reports: the salience of tax-related KAM disclosures influences multinational tax planning, highlighting broader consequences of this regulatory intervention.
                  Data Availability: Data are available from the public sources cited in the text.
                  JEL Classifications: H25; H26; H40.

papers.title: The Effect of Global Intangible Low-Taxed Income Tax on U.S. Multinational Companies’ Cross-Border Tangible Investments
papers.authors: Jingjing Huang, Benjamin Osswald, Ryan J. Wilson
papers.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  The Global Intangible Low-Taxed Income (GILTI) provision, enacted under the 2017 U.S. tax reform, aimed to deter profit shifting by U.S. multinational corporations (MNCs) but has raised concerns about unintended incentives to shift tangible investments abroad. Using an ex ante identification strategy based on public financial statements, we document that an average MNC increases foreign tangible investment by approximately $256.2 million relative to 2017 levels to minimize GILTI tax. Although this finding could raise concerns that firms are reducing domestic tangible investment for foreign expansion, we find no significant decline in domestic tangible investment. Furthermore, we find GILTI firms increase both foreign and domestic innovation, including capital-intensive technologies. The positive domestic innovation spillovers support the intended effect of the U.S. tax reform in boosting domestic economic growth. Our evidence reveals how international tax provisions, though aimed at curbing profit shifting, can simultaneously create unintended incentives.
                  JEL Classifications: M41; H25; H26.

papers.title: Choosing the Stage: The Strategic Role of Disclosure Venues in Guidance Revisions
papers.authors: Akash Chattopadhyay, Nayana Reiter, Mani Sethuraman
papers.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  When managers revise earnings guidance between earnings announcements, they choose not only what to disclose but also where to disclose—in a standalone release, a guidance call, an investor conference, or an analyst/investor (A/I) day. These venues differ in audience, format, and visibility, raising the question of whether venue choice is a strategic communication decision. In a large sample of unbundled revisions, we find that managers use calls for relatively large negative revisions and when litigation risk is higher and that they use conferences and A/I days for smaller revisions and when analyst disagreement is greater. Textual analysis reveals that calls feature cautious, litigious language for both upward and downward revisions, whereas conference and A/I day communications remain optimistic. In line with these framing differences, calls are associated with amplified reaction to negative news and are followed by more favorable earnings surprises, suggestive of effective expectation management, whereas conferences and A/I days are associated with muted reactions and reduced analyst dispersion and are followed by less favorable surprises. Our findings suggest that venue choice is a dimension of disclosure strategy for managers and an informative signal for investors.

papers.title: From Text to Beta: Macroeconomic Disclosures and Firm-Level Systematic Risk
papers.authors: Cameron Holstead, Alon Kalay, Gil Sadka, Federico Siano
papers.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  Using news text from The Wall Street Journal and macroeconomic disclosures in 10-K filings, we address the challenge of characterizing both time-varying aggregate risks and firm-level risk exposures. We develop a disclosure-based measure of systematic risk that (1) reveals salient macro risks in each period, (2) provides a text-based estimate of earnings exposure to these risks, and (3) explains the cross-section of stock returns. We also show that macro disclosures are pervasive across the annual report, grow over time, vary with the business cycle, and exhibit within-firm variation, consistent with the time-varying nature of systematic risk exposure. Overall, disclosures yield transparent and economically interpretable estimates of firm-level systematic risk.
                  Data Availability: Data are obtained from SEC filings, Bureau of Economic Analysis, The Wall Street Journal, Compustat, CRSP, I/B/E/S.
                  JEL Classifications: E31; E32; G11; G12; M21; M41.

papers.title: Building Better Information: Reporting Technology, Internal Information Frictions, and Investment Efficiency
papers.authors: Philip G. Berger, Feng Li, Lisa Yao Liu, M. H. Franco Wong
papers.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  We assess how firms use spending on reporting infrastructure to improve managerial reporting quality (MRQ) and whether doing so improves investment efficiency. Using the Sarbanes-Oxley Act’s internal control provisions (SOX 404) as a shock to MRQ demand, we find that treated firms increase reporting infrastructure spending, including for information technology and communications. We next examine variation across segments in the benefits and costs of improving reporting infrastructure. Segments increase spending more when facing larger internal moral hazard frictions and when they are less likely to have voluntarily improved MRQ before SOX (including segments insulated from competition, facing difficulty obtaining enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems, or lacking internal control personnel). Finally, we find that treated firms improve investment efficiency post-SOX 404, with larger gains among firms with higher spending on reporting infrastructure. Our findings indicate that regulatory mandates can improve investment efficiency by inducing reporting infrastructure improvements that enhance MRQ.
                  JEL Classifications: D83; G15; G18; G38; L15; M41; M42.

papers.title: Social Media Toxicity and Capital Markets
papers.authors: Elizabeth Blankespoor, Jedson Pinto, Kirti Sinha
papers.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  This paper asks about the existence, determinants, and implications of toxic content in financial social media. Using machine learning algorithms to measure toxicity in Seeking Alpha articles and comments, we find measurable toxicity concentrated primarily in user-generated comments rather than articles. Comment toxicity is greater for firms with more investor attention or uncertainty. We document three key results about toxicity in capital markets. First, toxicity displays a feedback loop in platform participation: past toxicity is associated with more future toxic contributors for a given firm. Second, firms receiving more toxic comments have greater retail trading volume but less informative retail trades, especially when comments disagree. Third, toxicity is associated with slower price discovery around earnings announcements. Our findings suggest that financial social media toxicity relates to both user behavior and market outcomes and raise important considerations for platform governance in financial markets.
                  Data Availability: The Seeking Alpha articles and comments used in this study were obtained directly from Seeking Alpha under a data-sharing arrangement and are proprietary; we are not permitted to redistribute them. These data may be requested from Seeking Alpha. Compustat, Execucomp, CRSP, and New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) Trade and Quote (TAQ) data are available through Wharton Research Data Services (WRDS) to subscribing institutions.
                  JEL Classifications: G14; G41; D83; D91.

papers.title: So similar, yet so different: comparing the US GAAP and IFRS experience at eliciting greater transparency on pension asset disclosures
papers.authors: Divya Anantharaman, Elizabeth Chuk, Tonni Shijun Xia
papers.abstract:
Abstract
                  We exploit two regulatory changes, one under US GAAP and the other under IFRS, that mandate improved disclosure of pension asset allocation. While the changes are otherwise similar, US GAAP retains the expected rate of return (“ERR”) on pension assets, which preparers can more easily manipulate if asset allocation remains opaque, while IFRS eliminates the ERR. We find that the IFRS standard improves pension asset transparency more than the US standard, which only mandates higher-quality disclosure without changing recognition or measurement and hence leaves unchanged preparers’ incentives to obfuscate. The US standard elicits a mixed response that reduces transparency in some respects. We isolate the relative deterioration in US firms’ transparency to firms with stronger incentives to inflate ERRs. Overall, our study highlights the potential for standard setters to learn from each other by comparing their regulatory experience on a specific accounting topic with clearly identifiable managerial incentives.

papers.title: The effect of the mandatory disclosure of corporate tax returns on reporting bias
papers.authors: ERIC J. ALLEN, HENRY L. FRIEDMAN, AYDIN UYSAL
papers.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  How do investor reactions to the mandatory disclosure of firm tax information influence managers' reporting choices? To answer this question, we build a structural model of reporting bias, which we test with a unique data set of Turkish firms that have been mandated to publicly disclose their tax returns since 2009. We find that both book and tax income numbers are informative to investors. Structural estimates are consistent with disclosure of the tax report reducing both market incentives to manage book earnings and investor uncertainty about underlying firm value. Tax disclosure is associated with higher reported tax income, though the increase is not statistically significant. Counterfactual estimates suggest that book‐tax‐conformity could change financial and tax reporting biases, but lead to a lower quality information environment relative to the separate disclosure of book and tax reports.
